batch.notes: These quotes come from scanned pages read by OCR. Compare each highlighted quote with the page image.

units.citation: Hey et al. (1995). Flood Reduction through Wetland Restoration: The Upper Mississippi River Basin as a Case History. Restoration Ecology.
units.quote:
The 1993 flood verifies the need for additional wetlands: the
amount of excess water that passed St. Louis during the 1993 flood
would have covered a
little more than 13 million acres—half of the wet-
land acreage drained since 1780 in the upper Mississippi Basin. By strate-
gically placing at least 13 million acres of wetlands on hydric soils in the
basin, we can solve the basin’s flooding problems in an ecologically
sound manner.

relationship.outcome_raw: a back-of-envelope storage calculation: the excess water that passed St. Louis in the 1993 flood would have covered a little more than 13 million acres (at deep-marsh depth), so placing at least 13 million acres of restored wetlands on hydric soils would solve the basin's flooding problems

context.practice_as_described: Wetland restoration: 'strategically placing at least 13 million acres of wetlands on hydric soils in the basin' (abstract), i.e. restoring riverine and palustrine wetlands on drained hydric soils (former beaver ponds and wetlands) by 'low-scale engineering techniques' so that they 'intercept and hold precipitation where it falls and store floodwaters where they occur' (abstract; p10). Mechanism: storage of excess flood volume at about a three-foot depth (deep marsh). BASELINE (comparator): the present drained and levee-confined basin (wetland area reduced from about 45 to under 20 million acres since 1780).
context.note: Commentary (Restoration Ecology 3(1):4-17), not a hydrological study. The 13-million-acre figure is a storage-volume calculation (p10: 111 million acre-feet passed St. Louis in 80 days; bank-full discharge 450,000 cfs; excess approximately 40 million acre-feet; 'Distributed at a three-foot depth (the approximate depth of a deep marsh), these waters would have covereda little more than 13 million acres'). No flood routing, no peak/stage modelling, no siting: the authors say 'Hydrologically, of course, this argument is incomplete. The key to the effectiveness of an additional 13 million acres of flood storage is in its location' (p11) and 'Generating the figure of 13 million acres involved some facile number crunching ... The hard work - producing the hydrologic assessments and computer analyses - remains to be done' (p12). Treat as a volume-capacity estimate (STAGE/VOLUME, not PEAK). Severity cue from p5: 'Such a land area, it appears, could have easily contained most of the floodwaters that devastated the valley in 1993.' Magnitude from p10 and p13 ('If the 100-year flood flow, as recorded in 1993, were to be treated'). claim_basis=modelled per lane brief; strength left unspecified (no reduction metric).

units.citation: Fiener et al. (2005). Managing erosion and water quality in agricultural watersheds by small detention ponds. Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment.
units.quote:
The detention
ponds had a volume of 30-260 m* ha' and trapped 54-85% of the incoming sediment

relationship.outcome_raw: the detention ponds trapped 54-85% of the incoming sediment

context.practice_as_described: Small dry detention ponds at field borders: where runoff concentrates in slope depressions and overtops the downslope field border, the border was raised by earth embankments (1.25-1.66 m high at the pour point) to create a detention pond holding water only during storms, drained by a perforated standpipe into an underground tile outlet with an orifice plate; outflow routed through a grassed waterway or pipes to the toe slope (p2 abstract; p4-5). Fields upslope farmed under integrated farming with mulch tillage and mustard cover crops (potato - winter wheat - maize - winter wheat rotation) (p3). BASELINE (comparator): sediment entering the pond from the upslope field (inflow vs delivered sediment), i.e. without the pond the incoming sediment would leave the field.
context.note: Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment 110:132-142. OCR'd scan; body pages are two-column and interleaved in the text layer, so all quotes come from the single-column abstract (cached PDF p2; p1 is a repository cover page). Trapping efficiency = deposited / incoming sediment, measured with erosion pins and outflow samplers. Per p8 (interleaved, not quotable) the 54-85% was measured in 1993 only (first year after landscape redesign, 15 major erosion events; total trapping up to 15.3 t/ha/yr); after dredging in early 1994 sedimentation became too small to measure because on-site mulch-tillage erosion control became effective, and the authors estimate long-term trapping at about 50-80% (p8, p11). Sediment trapping (54-85%) exceeded nutrient trapping (35-70%) because delivered sediment was enriched in fines (p8; the line is interleaved with Fig. 4 labels, not quotable). Pond volume is 30-260 m3 per ha of watershed.

units.citation: Fiener et al. (2005). Managing erosion and water quality in agricultural watersheds by small detention ponds. Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment.
units.quote:
Due to the siltation of the pond bottom,
the short filled time (1-5 days) and the small water covered area, infiltration and evaporation reduced runoff by less than 10% for
large events.

relationship.outcome_raw: infiltration and evaporation in the ponds reduced runoff volume by less than 10% for large events, because the pond bottom silts up, ponds are filled only briefly (1-5 days) and the water-covered area is small

context.practice_as_described: Small dry detention ponds at field borders: where runoff concentrates in slope depressions and overtops the downslope field border, the border was raised by earth embankments (1.25-1.66 m high at the pour point) to create a detention pond holding water only during storms, drained by a perforated standpipe into an underground tile outlet with an orifice plate; outflow routed through a grassed waterway or pipes to the toe slope (p2 abstract; p4-5). Fields upslope farmed under integrated farming with mulch tillage and mustard cover crops (potato - winter wheat - maize - winter wheat rotation) (p3). BASELINE (comparator): inflow volume to the pond (water balance: inflow vs outflow plus infiltration and evaporation).
context.note: Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment 110:132-142. OCR'd scan; body pages are two-column and interleaved in the text layer, so all quotes come from the single-column abstract (cached PDF p2; p1 is a repository cover page). Near-null volume effect, kept as such. Encoded as narrative because the source gives only an upper bound ('less than'). The conclusions (p11, interleaved) state 'no significant reduction of runoff volume can be expected'; the example event at pond P02 (p10) gave a 10% volume reduction, described as the maximum to expect for all ponds. Contrast with the large peak-flow effect (ev_flood_hazard_fien05_1): the ponds delay and attenuate runoff, they do not remove it.

units.citation: Fiener et al. (2005). Managing erosion and water quality in agricultural watersheds by small detention ponds. Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment.
units.quote: Peak runoff during heavy rains was lowered bya factor of three.

relationship.outcome_raw: peak runoff rate leaving the field during heavy rains was lowered by a factor of three by temporary storage in the detention ponds (fold change with no baseline in the quote: direction only)

context.practice_as_described: Small dry detention ponds at field borders: where runoff concentrates in slope depressions and overtops the downslope field border, the border was raised by earth embankments (1.25-1.66 m high at the pour point) to create a detention pond holding water only during storms, drained by a perforated standpipe into an underground tile outlet with an orifice plate; outflow routed through a grassed waterway or pipes to the toe slope (p2 abstract; p4-5). Fields upslope farmed under integrated farming with mulch tillage and mustard cover crops (potato - winter wheat - maize - winter wheat rotation) (p3). BASELINE (comparator): peak inflow rate into the pond (computed from the storage water balance) vs measured peak outflow.
context.note: Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment 110:132-142. OCR'd scan; body pages are two-column and interleaved in the text layer, so all quotes come from the single-column abstract (cached PDF p2; p1 is a repository cover page). Mechanism: temporary storage of 200-500 m3 of runoff behind the raised field border, released through a throttled tile outlet (abstract; p5). Flood here = on-farm and downstream runoff peaks / muddy floods at field-watershed scale (1.6-7.8 ha), not river flooding. Fold change direction-only per the 2026-10-20 ruling; the baseline exists in the body (p9: P02 peak 'reduced from 15.1 to' a value the OCR renders as '4.91s—'' [about 4.9 l/s]) but the outflow number is OCR-garbled, so it is not used. Response range: dampening approaches zero for broad snowmelt peaks (p9, interleaved), and 'during the study period no events with a re-occurrence time >5 years were observed' (p10, interleaved), so the effect is untested in larger floods; the authors expect lower efficacy in larger events without on-site soil conservation (p10). hazard_magnitude not stated in the abstract; the largest events were one of the 10 heaviest of 1423 rains (43.3 mm, 5 June 1995, p7).

units.quote:
There is strong evidence that wetlands evaporate more 
water that other land types, such as forests, savannah 
grassland or arable land. Two thirds of studies (48 of 
74) conclude that wetlands increase average annual 
evaporation or reduce average annual river flow. About 
10% of studies (7) conclude the opposite; for example 
some woodlands in Zambia had greater evaporation than 
the adjacent wetlands. The remaining 25% are neutral. 
There is no obvious distinction amongst different 
wetland sub-types or geographical regions of the world.

units.quote:
Two-thirds of studies (47 of 71) conclude that wetlands 
reduce the flow of water in downstream rivers during 
dry periods. Evidence is mainly from North America 
and Europe, but includes floodplains in Sierra Leone 
and wetlands in Southern Africa. This is backed by 
overwhelming evidence (22 of 23 studies) that shows 
evaporation from wetlands to be higher than from non- 
wetland portions of the catchment during dry periods. 
There is no discernible difference for different wetland 
sub-types. In 20% of cases, wetlands increase river 
flows during the dry season.

of floodplains conclude that flow variability is reduced by

reduced.
